title: Seljuks and the Georgian Golden Age
subtitle: AD 1064–1243 · The Great Turkish Invasion, David the Builder, Queen Tamar, Zakarid Armenia, Nizami and the Mongol Arrival

categories.label: Power
categories.subtitle: The Georgian kings from Giorgi II to Rusudan, the Zakarid princes of Armenia, the Eldiguzid atabegs and the Shirvanshahs

entries.label: Giorgi II and the Seljuk tribute
entries.hint: Giorgi II became king of Georgia in 1072 at the age of seventeen and had to deal with Seljuk raids that devastated the land, until the invasion of Malik-Shah in 1080 forced him to pay tribute. He abdicated in 1089 in favour of his sixteen-year-old son David IV.
entries.note: Kartlis Tskhovreba (Life of David, Matiane Kartlisa); Stephen Rapp, Georgian Christian Identity (2003).

entries.label: David IV the Builder
entries.hint: David IV 'the Builder' (Aghmashenebeli) restored the kingdom: he reformed the army, settled Kipchak warriors, crushed the Seljuk coalition at Didgori in 1121, took Tbilisi in 1122 and made it his capital, and brought Shirvan and the Armenian city of Ani under his control; he built Gelati monastery and its academy. Georgians remember his reign as the beginning of their golden age.
entries.note: Matiane Kartlisa, 'The Life of David, King of Kings'; Rapp 2003; Cyril Toumanoff, Studies in Christian Caucasian History (1963).

entries.label: Demetre I and Giorgi III
entries.hint: David's son Demetre I (1125–1156) took Ganja in 1139 and held the realm against dynastic revolts, and Giorgi III (1156–1184) took Ani again and Arran in successive campaigns, fought the Eldiguzid atabegs and strengthened royal authority; at the end of his reign he made his daughter Tamar co-ruler in 1178.
entries.note: Kartlis Tskhovreba; Rapp 2003.

entries.label: Queen Tamar
entries.hint: Tamar, crowned co-ruler in 1178 and queen in her own right in 1184, was the first woman to rule Georgia and styled herself 'king of kings'; she put down aristocratic revolts, won victories at Shamkor (1195) and Basiani (1203), brought into her sphere the Armenian lands to the Araxes, Shirvan and the Empire of Trebizond, and presided over the flowering of Georgian literature and art. She died in 1213.
entries.note: The Life of Tamar (Basil Ezosmodzghvari); Kartlis Tskhovreba; Rapp 2003.

entries.label: Giorgi IV Lasha and Rusudan
entries.hint: Giorgi IV Lasha (1213–1223), Tamar's son, was wounded at Khunani against the Mongol raiders in 1221 and died soon after; his sister Rusudan (1223–1245) saw the Khwarazmian conquest of Tbilisi in 1226 and, after 1236, the Mongol occupation, which broke the golden age.
entries.note: Kartlis Tskhovreba; Rapp 2003.

entries.group: Zakarid Armenia and the Khachen Princes
entries.label: The Zakarids, Georgian generals and Armenian princes
entries.hint: Sargis Zakarian's sons Zakare and Ivane Mkhargrdzeli, of an Armenian family partly drawn into the Georgian church, led Tamar's armies as amirspasalars, took Ani in 1199 and ruled much of northern and central Armenia as Georgian vassals, with their own princely courts, church building and patronage. Ani prospered again in the thirteenth century.
entries.note: Kirakos Gandzaketsi, History of the Armenians; Stepanos Orbelian; Hewsen, Armenia: A Historical Atlas (2001).

entries.group: Zakarid Armenia and the Khachen Princes
entries.label: Hasan-Jalal and the princes of Khachen
entries.hint: In the mountains of Artsakh (Karabakh) the princes of Khachen, descendants of the old Albanian lines, kept an Armenian-speaking Christian principality under various suzerains; Hasan-Jalal Dawla, prince of Khachen from about 1214, built the monastery of Gandzasar in 1216–1238, which became the see of the Albanian catholicosate. The principality survived the Mongol invasion by submission.
entries.note: Kirakos Gandzaketsi; Gandzasar inscriptions; Hewsen 2001.

entries.label: The Shirvanshahs of Shamakhi
entries.hint: Under Manuchihr III (c. 1120–1160) and Akhsitan I (c. 1160–1196), the Shirvanshahs of the Kasranid line held the lands between the Kura and the Caspian from Shamakhi and later Baku, as vassals of the Seljuks and then of Georgia, and made their court a centre of Persian poetry; the poet Khaqani was their panegyrist.
entries.note: Minorsky, A History of Sharvan and Darband (1958); Khaqani, Divan.

entries.label: The Eldiguzid atabegs of Azerbaijan
entries.hint: Shams al-Din Eldiguz, a Kipchak slave of the Seljuk sultan and then atabeg, founded about 1136 a dynasty that governed Azerbaijan, Arran and western Iran in the sultans' name and then independently, with its seats at Nakhchivan, Tabriz and Hamadan; its rulers Jahan Pahlavan, Qizil Arslan and Abu Bakr were the main Muslim rivals of Georgia until the Khwarazmians took their lands in 1225.
entries.note: Ibn al-Athir, al-Kamil; Minorsky, Studies in Caucasian History (1953); C. E. Bosworth, The Islamic Dynasties (1967).

categories.label: Conflict
categories.subtitle: The invasion of 1080, Didgori and the taking of Tbilisi, Shamkor and Basiani, and the Mongol and Khwarazmian blows

entries.label: The Great Turkish Invasion
entries.hint: In 1080 Malik-Shah's Seljuk army and Turkmen followers invaded Georgia, devastating Kartli and Samtskhe, plundering and burning; the Georgian chroniclers call it the 'Great Turkish Invasion' (Didi Turkoba) and describe how for a decade the Turkmen wintered in the land while the peasants fled to the mountains. Giorgi II had to submit and pay tribute.
entries.note: Matiane Kartlisa (Life of David); Rapp 2003.

entries.label: Didgori
entries.hint: On 12 August 1121 David IV with a Georgian army of some 56,000 men, with Kipchak horsemen and a corps of some hundred Frankish knights, destroyed in the gorge of Didgori a much larger coalition of Seljuk and Turkmen forces under Najm al-Din Il-ghazi of Mardin, according to Georgian and Arabic sources. The battle freed the country and opened the way to Tbilisi.
entries.note: Matiane Kartlisa; Ibn al-Qalanisi; Ibn al-Athir; Rapp 2003.

entries.label: The capture of Tbilisi
entries.hint: In 1122 David IV took Tbilisi from its Muslim emir after a siege, ending the emirate that had held it since 737, and made it his capital; the city kept its mosques and Muslim population and the king the title 'king of the Abkhazians, Kartvelians, Rans, Kakhs and Armenians, Shirvanshah and Shahanshah'.
entries.note: Matiane Kartlisa; Ibn al-Azraq; Rapp 2003.

entries.label: The taking of Ganja and its gates
entries.hint: After an earthquake had destroyed Ganja in September 1139, Demetre I of Georgia took the ruined city and carried off its great iron gates to Gelati, where they remained until the twentieth century. The ravaged city was re-founded as Gandzak and became the home of the poet Nizami.
entries.note: Matiane; Ibn al-Athir; Kirakos Gandzaketsi.

entries.label: Shamkor and Basiani
entries.hint: In 1195 the Georgian army of Queen Tamar, under the amirspasalar Zakare, routed the atabeg Abu Bakr's Muslim army at Shamkor and took Ganja; in 1203 at Basiani, near Erzurum, they destroyed the army of the Seljuk sultan of Rum and its allies. The victories made Georgia the strongest power of the region.
entries.note: Kartlis Tskhovreba (Life of Tamar); Ibn al-Athir; Rapp 2003.

entries.label: Jebe and Subutai in the Caucasus
entries.hint: A Mongol army of 20,000 men under Jebe and Subutai pursuing the Khwarazmshah entered Azerbaijan and Arran in 1220–1221, destroyed Georgian forces at Khunani in 1221 and crossed the Caucasus by Derbent, defeating the Alans and Kipchaks and the Russian princes at the Kalka in 1223. Giorgi Lasha died of a wound in 1223.
entries.note: Kartlis Tskhovreba; Ibn al-Athir; Kirakos Gandzaketsi; John Andrew Boyle (ed.), Cambridge History of Iran, vol. 5 (1968).

entries.label: Jalal ad-Din in Georgia
entries.hint: The Khwarazmian sultan Jalal ad-Din Mingburnu, driven from India by the Mongols, defeated the Georgians at Garni in 1225 and took Tbilisi in March 1226, where he ordered the massacre of the Christian population, according to Georgian sources and Nasawi his secretary. His rule broke the Georgian monarchy's strength.
entries.note: Kartlis Tskhovreba; Nasawi, Sirat Jalal al-Din; Kirakos Gandzaketsi.

entries.label: The Mongol conquest
entries.hint: In 1236 the Mongol general Chormaghan began the conquest of Georgia, Armenia and Azerbaijan, taking Tbilisi and Ani in 1236 and forcing Queen Rusudan to flee to Kutaisi; in 1243 the victory at Köse Dağ over the Seljuk sultan of Rum completed the subjugation of the highlands to the Ilkhanate.
entries.note: Kirakos Gandzaketsi, History 21–22; Juvaini, History of the World Conqueror; Boyle 1968.

categories.label: Order
categories.subtitle: The council of Ruisi-Urbnisi, the Kipchak army, the charter of the vizier and the Armenian law code

entries.label: The council of Ruisi-Urbnisi
entries.hint: The church council of Ruisi-Urbnisi in 1103 called by David IV reorganised the church, removing unworthy clergy and bringing the church under the king's authority; the archbishop of Chqondidi, Giorgi, became the king's chancellor. It was a base of his centralisation.
entries.note: Matiane Kartlisa; Rapp 2003.

entries.label: The Kipchak army and the king's guard
entries.hint: David IV settled in Kartli some tens of thousands of families of Kipchak (Qipchaq) nomads from the north Caucasian steppe, who owed military service in return for land, and made a standing royal army and guard (Monaspa) loyal to himself in place of the feudal levies, a force which gave him his military advantage against the Seljuks.
entries.note: Matiane Kartlisa; Rapp 2003; Peter Golden, Khazar Studies (1980).

entries.label: The Armenian law code of Mkhitar Gosh
entries.hint: The scholar and abbot Mkhitar Gosh compiled in 1184 the Datastanagirk, the Armenian law code, a collection of canon, Roman-Byzantine, Syrian and customary law for the Armenians under Georgian and Seljuk rule, which was used until the nineteenth century, in the Armenian communities of the diaspora.
entries.note: Mkhitar Gosh, Datastanagirk; Robert Thomson, The Lawcode [Datastanagirk] of Mxit'ar Goš (2000).

entries.label: Tamar's council and the vizier
entries.hint: Under Tamar the government was directed by a council, the Karavi, and the vizier, with the high offices of mtsignobartukhutsesi (chancellor), amirspasalar (commander) and mechurchletukhutsesi (treasurer), and with the nobility as a power held in check by the royal army; the offices continued the Byzantine and Persian patterns and ran a bureaucracy that wrote in Georgian, Greek, Persian and Armenian.
entries.note: Kartlis Tskhovreba (Life of Tamar); Rapp 2003.

categories.label: Belief
categories.subtitle: The Georgian church reforms, Gelati and Vardzia, the Armenian Chalcedonians and the Georgian houses in Jerusalem

entries.label: The Georgian houses in Jerusalem and Athos
entries.hint: Georgian monarchs supported the Monastery of the Cross at Jerusalem, where Rustaveli was said to have been a treasurer and is shown in a fresco, the Georgian houses at Mount Athos, Mount Sinai and Antioch, and a system of pilgrim and learned exchange. Tamar sent alms to the Holy Land, and Georgian tradition says she offered a ransom for the True Cross after Hattin.
entries.note: Monastery of the Cross, Jerusalem (Rustaveli fresco); Rapp 2003.

entries.label: Gelati
entries.hint: David IV founded Gelati near Kutaisi in 1106 as a monastery, burial place and academy, a 'second Jerusalem' and an 'another Athos', with a mosaic of the Virgin and frescoes of kings; he was buried in the gateway in 1125 so that all who entered would walk over his grave. UNESCO lists it as a World Heritage Site (1994).
entries.note: Matiane Kartlisa; UNESCO World Heritage no. 710 (1994); Rapp 2003.

entries.label: Armenian Chalcedonians and the Zakarid church
entries.hint: The Zakarids, who adopted the Chalcedonian creed of the Georgian Church while remaining Armenian-speakers, built Armenian-style monasteries, among them Haghpat, Sanahin and Harichavank, and Chalcedonian Armenian communities stayed in the Georgian communion, in a divided religious landscape which later chronicles narrate.
entries.note: Kirakos Gandzaketsi; Stepanos Orbelian; Hewsen 2001.

categories.label: Expression
categories.subtitle: Gelati, Vardzia, the Armenian monasteries of the Zakarids and the Knight in the Panther's Skin

entries.label: Vardzia
entries.hint: The cave city of Vardzia, begun under Giorgi III in 1156 and extended by Tamar, was cut into the rock face above the Kura valley in some thousands of rooms and a church of the Dormition with wall-paintings, which include portraits of Giorgi III and Tamar, making it a fortress-monastery of the southern frontier; an earthquake in 1283 brought down much of the outer face.
entries.note: Vardzia inscriptions and frescoes; Rapp 2003.

entries.label: The Armenian monasteries of the Zakarids
entries.hint: The Zakarid and Khachen princes built the Armenian monastic complexes of Haghartsin, Goshavank (founded by Mkhitar Gosh after the earthquake of 1188), Gandzasar (1216–1238) and Noravank, with domed churches, gavits, and reliefs and cross-stones, in a last great phase of medieval Armenian architecture under Georgian suzerainty.
entries.note: Monastery inscriptions; Der Nersessian, Armenian Art (1977).

entries.label: The Knight in the Panther's Skin
entries.hint: Shota Rustaveli, treasurer of Queen Tamar according to tradition, wrote in about 1200 the epic poem Vepkhistqaosani ('The Man in the Panther's Skin'), 1,600 quatrains of verse on the friendship of Tariel and Avtandil and the love of the knight, which became the Georgian national poem and which the Georgians recite and illustrate; the dedication names Tamar.
entries.note: Shota Rustaveli, Vepkhistqaosani (trans. R. Stevenson, 1977); Rapp 2003.

categories.label: Thought
categories.subtitle: Rustaveli, Petritsi and the Gelati school, Nizami and Khaqani, Mkhitar Gosh and the fable

entries.label: Ioane Petritsi and the Gelati academy
entries.hint: Ioane Petritsi, a Georgian scholar who had studied in Constantinople, taught philosophy at the Gelati academy and translated and commented on Proclus's Elements of Theology, with a Neoplatonic outlook; his work is a high point of Georgian philosophical writing and a link to the Byzantine Platonist school.
entries.note: Ioane Petritsi, Commentary on Proclus's Elements of Theology (ed. S. Kaukhchishvili); Rapp 2003.

entries.label: Khaqani of Shirvan
entries.hint: The court poet of the Shirvanshahs Khaqani, whose Divan and travel poem Tuhfat al-Iraqayn on his pilgrimage to Mecca and Iraq are in a dense, learned and difficult Persian style, wrote in the service of Manuchihr III and Akhsitan I, and was imprisoned for a time in Shirvan.
entries.note: Khaqani, Divan and Tuhfat al-Iraqayn; Minorsky 1958.

entries.label: Mkhitar Gosh and the Fables
entries.hint: Mkhitar Gosh, born at Gandzak about 1130, was a monk and teacher who compiled the Datastanagirk and a collection of 190 fables in the classical Armenian, one of the first literary works in the vernacular of the time, and founded the monastery of Nor Getik, later Goshavank, with its school.
entries.note: Mkhitar Gosh, Fables (ed. Orbeli; trans. R. Thomson); Thomson 2000.

entries.label: The chronicles of the golden age
entries.hint: The Georgian chronicles of David (Matiane Kartlisa), of the 'Life of David, King of Kings' about 1130, and of Tamar (Basil Ezosmodzghvari, the 'History and Eulogies of the Sovereigns') about 1210, with the poetry of Chakhrukhadze and Shavteli praising Tamar, record the age in a mixture of history and panegyric.
entries.note: Kartlis Tskhovreba; Chakhrukhadze, Tamariani; Ioane Shavteli, Abdulmesia; Rapp 2003.

entries.label: Nizami of Ganja
entries.hint: Nizami Ganjavi, born at Ganja about 1141 and working at the courts of the Shaddadids, Eldiguzids and Shirvanshahs, wrote in Persian the five poems of the Khamsa, Makhzan al-asrar, Khusraw and Shirin, Layla and Majnun, the Haft Paykar and the Iskandarnameh, the greatest romantic epics of Persian literature. He died about 1209.
entries.note: Nizami, Khamsa (ed. Dastgerdi); Julie Scott Meisami, The Haft Paykar (1995).

categories.label: Economy
categories.subtitle: Tbilisi's commerce, Georgian coinage, the vineyards of Kakheti and the spoils of war

entries.label: Georgian coinage and the royal estates
entries.hint: David IV and his successors minted copper and silver coins of Byzantine and Arabic types, with Georgian and Arabic legends and Tamar's silver dirhams carry the queen's name in Arabic and the royal title; the crown, the Church and the nobles shared the lands, and the king drew on spoils of war and tribute.
entries.note: Georgian numismatics (D. Kapanadze, Georgian Numismatics, 1969); Rapp 2003.

entries.label: Tbilisi and the Georgian trade
entries.hint: Tbilisi, with its sulphur baths, caravanserais, craftsmen's quarters and Muslim, Christian and Jewish merchants, was a trading entrepôt on the road from the Black Sea to the Caspian and Persia, and the Georgian kings drew revenues from the commercial dues, the royal estates and the tribute of vassal states.
entries.note: Georgian chronicles; Rapp 2003; Minorsky 1958.

categories.label: Technology
categories.subtitle: The cave city of Vardzia and the engineering of the Zakarid monasteries

entries.label: The hydraulic system of Vardzia
entries.hint: Vardzia drew water from springs by a network of channels and cisterns inside the rock, had a hidden approach by tunnels and a series of terraces for gardens, and a pharmacy, bakeries and wine cellars; its engineers cut some 3,000 rooms, according to common estimates, in thirteen levels.
entries.note: Vardzia surveys (Georgian National Museum); Rapp 2003.

categories.label: Exchange
categories.subtitle: The Kipchak settlement, the crusader contacts and the Black Sea alliance with Trebizond

entries.label: The Kipchaks in Georgia
entries.hint: The Kipchak families who settled in Georgia at David's invitation, and the further numbers of Turkic nomads and slaves who entered the Caucasus, gave Georgia a Turkic element whose language and customs left traces in military terms; the Kipchaks became Christian and entered the Georgian nobility.
entries.note: Matiane Kartlisa; Golden 1980.

entries.label: Trebizond and the crusaders
entries.hint: In April 1204 Tamar's army supported her kinsmen Alexios and David Komnenos in seizing Trebizond and founding the Empire of Trebizond, in a move that gave Georgia a Black Sea ally and protégé; her court also had dealings with the crusader states and the Latin Church.
entries.note: Kartlis Tskhovreba (Life of Tamar); Michael Panaretos; Rapp 2003.

categories.label: World
categories.subtitle: The Ganja earthquake and the Mongol shadow

entries.label: The Ganja earthquake of 1139
entries.hint: A great earthquake on 30 September 1139 destroyed Ganja in Arran and killed tens of thousands according to the chroniclers, who give figures of up to 230,000; the quake also created Lake Göygöl. It was the greatest natural disaster of the Caucasus in the Middle Ages.
entries.note: Ibn al-Athir 11; Kirakos Gandzaketsi; Ibn al-Jawzi.

entries.label: The Mongol shadow
entries.hint: The Georgian golden age ended in the same two generations in which the Mongol empire reached from China to the Danube; the raids of 1221 and the conquest of 1236–1243 made the Caucasus a province of a world empire and ended the independence of its kingdoms.
entries.note: Boyle 1968; Rapp 2003.

categories.label: Lives
categories.subtitle: The queen who ruled as king, a Kipchak slave girl who became a poet's wife and the people of a captured Tbilisi

entries.label: Afaq, Nizami's Kipchak wife
entries.hint: Nizami's wife Afaq was a Kipchak slave girl given to him by the ruler of Derbent, who became his wife and the mother of his son Muhammad; he mourns her death in Khusraw and Shirin.
entries.note: Nizami, Khusraw and Shirin; Meisami 1995.

entries.label: Tamar, king of kings
entries.hint: Georgian writers address Tamar as 'king' (mepe) in the masculine, a title which she used for herself, and her court poets, Chakhrukhadze and Shavteli, praise her as a sun-like ruler; her two marriages, to Yuri Bogolyubsky of Rus and then to the Ossetian prince David Soslan, are narrated by the Georgian chroniclers. She was the first woman to rule Georgia in her own right.
entries.note: Chakhrukhadze, Tamariani; Kartlis Tskhovreba (Life of Tamar); Rapp 2003.

entries.label: The people of Tbilisi in 1226
entries.hint: According to Georgian and Persian sources, when Jalal ad-Din took Tbilisi he demanded of the Christians that they trample the icons of the Church of Sioni, and killed those who refused; Nasawi says the Khwarazmians slaughtered the population. The numbers are not known.
entries.note: Kartlis Tskhovreba; Nasawi, Sirat Jalal al-Din.
